title: Answering Modalism

keyTerms.d: The teaching that God is a single divine person who is revealed in three modes, roles, or manifestations — anciently pictured as successive (Father in creation, Son in redemption, Spirit in the church). On either view there are not three who are God; there is one who is God, appearing under three titles. In the early centuries it was called monarchianism (jealousy for God’s sole monarchia), and more specifically modalistic monarchianism or Sabellianism, after Sabellius, a teacher active in Rome in the early third century.

“The Father suffers.” Because modalism makes the Father the one who suffers on the cross — there being no distinct Son to do the suffering — it earned this mocking label. The historic faith denies it: the divine nature does not suffer or die, and the Father was not crucified; the seat of the Son’s suffering is the genuine humanity he assumed.

Modalism’s largest modern form, out of the “New Issue” controversy among American Pentecostals around 1913–1916. Its most influential systematic theologian is David K. Bernard of the United Pentecostal Church International. Bernard affirms one God and the absolute deity of Jesus Christ, and holds that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are real — but as “manifestations, modes, offices, or relationships” of the one God, not three distinct persons; he locates the deity of the Son in the indwelling Father, so that the prayers and submissions of Jesus express the relation of his genuine humanity to the deity dwelling in him. It is held by many who are sincere and devout.

Latin theology’s enduring formula — una substantia, tres personae — from Tertullian’s Against Praxeas (c. AD 210–213), the first sustained defence of trinitarian distinctions. He called the three distinct “not in condition, but in degree” (gradus, “step” or order of relation), “not in substance, but in form.” Order, not rank: not that the Son or Spirit is God to a lesser degree — the creedal faith holds the three co-equal and co-eternal, one in substance and power.

The decisive text, because it reaches behind the incarnation altogether. The petitioner asks for “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (17:5) and says “you loved me before the foundation of the world” (17:24). Jesus does not say he was foreknown; he says he had glory “with you” — a shared possession, not a place in a plan. Love between Father and Son before the world began is eternal interpersonal fact, the very thing a mode can never be.

The one God has one undivided will. The two wills orthodoxy confesses are in the incarnate Christ, by his two natures. So in Gethsemane “not my will, but yours” is the Son’s genuine human will freely yielding to the divine will he eternally shares with the Father — not two divine wills, still less two gods. The incarnate Son, a person truly distinct from the Father, genuinely submits; that is the point against modalism.

Polytheism counts gods by separable essences — Zeus and Poseidon are two because they have two distinct natures, two wills, divisible turf, and can act against one another. The persons of the Trinity have one undivided divine essence, one will, one power; nothing is parcelled out among them. The Son is not a second instance of deity; he is the one God, eternally the Son. This is why the church rejected tritheism wherever it appeared.

keyTerms.t: Social vs classical trinitarianism (reported, not adjudicated)
keyTerms.d: An internal, intra-Christian debate about how to state the doctrine — not whether modalism is an error. Cornelius Plantinga and others defend social-trinitarian language of three “centers of consciousness,” while Brian Leftow and Karen Kilby argue that overemphasising the distinctness of the persons concedes too much to the modalist’s complaint. The site reports the dispute without taking a side; it shows the Oneness concern is taken seriously even by those who reject the Oneness conclusion.

derive.q: In Gethsemane Jesus falls on his face and prays, “not as I will, but as you will.” On modalism — one person wearing the masks of Father and Son — to whom is he praying?
derive.ans: to no one but himself — the prayer becomes theater
derive.why: Keep the prayers real and you have two who commune, which is the doctrine. If Father and Son are one person, every prayer of Jesus is either theater — a performance with no listener — or a man addressing himself in agony. The anti-modalism point rests on the real address: the Son prays to the Father, real address to one who is really other.

derive.q: At the Jordan the Son comes up from the water, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice from heaven says, “This is my beloved Son.” Can one actor wear all three masks at once and converse across them?
derive.ans: no — a single actor changes masks between scenes
derive.why: Three distinct presences, at one moment, with one of them speaking about another. Successive modes cannot share one scene; persons can act together. And omnipresence does not rescue it: it explains how one person can be in three places, not how he can, in the same moment, speak from heaven to another as “my beloved Son” and be the Son who is spoken of.

derive.q: Challenged on his testimony, Jesus invokes the law requiring two witnesses: “I bear witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me” (John 8:17–18). On the modalist count, how many witnesses?
derive.ans: one — and Jesus’ own argument collapses
derive.why: One person in two roles is a single witness testifying twice. The argument works only if Father and Son are genuinely two. (If the reply is that the two are Jesus’ deity and his humanity, the law counts the testimony of two people — and natures do not testify; persons do.)

derive.q: Oneness teachers say the glory of John 17:5 existed only in God’s plan. But what does Jesus actually say he had, and with whom?
derive.ans: glory he had WITH the Father — a shared possession, not a place in a plan
derive.why: He does not say he was foreknown; he says he had glory “with you” before the world existed. The one praying speaks of a relationship that obtained before any human nature existed to do the addressing — so the petitioner cannot be the human nature speaking to indwelling deity; he is the pre-existent divine Son. That is eternal interpersonal fact, the one thing a mode can never be.

derive.q: Grant that modalism really does save the oneness of God. What does it spend to do it?
derive.ans: the gospel’s central relationship — the eternal love of Father and Son
derive.why: “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and the Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world; the Trinity lets those texts stand together, so God’s love neither waits on creation nor divides the God who is one — modalism has no eternal Beloved to point to. And salvation is adoption into the Son’s communion with the Father; on the modalist account there is nowhere to bring us. In saving the oneness, modalism spends the relationship the gospel exists to share.

honestState.p1: The argument clears the charge it takes up: modalism cannot make sense of the biblical data — the simultaneous baptism, the Son’s real address to the Father, the two witnesses, and the glory shared with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5). What the reply does NOT claim to do is dissolve the mystery. It answers the “three gods” (tritheism) charge; it does not pretend to comprehend how one being is three persons — and orthodoxy concedes that. The analogies all limp: water’s three states are actually modalism (the same water, usually one at a time); three men sharing humanity are actually tritheism.
honestState.fairness: Oneness theology is stated at full strength, not caricatured: Bernard affirms one God and the absolute deity of Jesus Christ, and Oneness believers are sincere and devout. The “three gods” objection’s ablest contemporary exponent, the analytic philosopher Dale Tuggy (author of the Stanford Encyclopedia “Trinity” entry), presses a version of it — stated as his, and toward a strict unitarianism in which God is the Father alone — which is a reminder that whatever answers the charge must not collapse the three back into one person. There is real and respectful engagement here: the Oneness–Trinitarian Pentecostal Dialogue (2002–2007) and critical assessments by Gregory Boyd, a former Oneness believer. And within orthodoxy itself there is a live, reported-not-adjudicated debate about how to STATE the doctrine (Plantinga’s social trinitarianism vs. Leftow and Kilby).
honestState.verdict: Across the confessional spectrum — Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant — there is no live dispute that modalism falls outside Nicene orthodoxy; that judgment was settled in the third and fourth centuries and has never been seriously reopened. Modalism holds fast to one true thing — that there is one God — and its jealousy for monotheism is honoured, not abandoned. But it secures the oneness at a price Scripture will not let it pay: it must turn the Son’s prayers into soliloquy, the Father’s voice at the Jordan into ventriloquism, and the eternal love of Father for Son into nothing at all. So modalism is a serious error, as the historic church has judged: one God, undivided in being; three coequal, coeternal, genuinely distinct persons, eternally in love.

order: Modalism teaches that Father, Son and Spirit are one divine person in three modes or roles — not three who are God, but one who is God under three titles (today’s Oneness theology: simultaneous manifestations of the one omnipresent God).

Scripture stages simultaneous, interpersonal relations the theory cannot survive: the baptism (three at once, one speaking about another), the Son praying to the Father, the Father and Son as two witnesses, and glory shared with the Father before the world existed (John 17:5).

Therefore the persons of the one God are really and eternally distinct — one undivided essence, three persons, never three gods — and modalism, in saving the oneness, loses the gospel’s central relationship. Modalism is a serious error, as the historic church has judged.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: Modalism teaches that Father, Son and Spirit are one divine person in three modes or roles — not three who are God, but one who is God under three titles (ancient: successive; Oneness today: simultaneous manifestations of the one omnipresent God). Precision: its motive, jealousy for monotheism, is not a vice — it is half of the truth the doctrine of the Trinity is built to protect.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: Scripture stages simultaneous, interpersonal relations the theory cannot survive — the baptism, the Son praying to the Father, two witnesses, glory shared with the Father before the world existed. Precision: the texts that resist modalism are not a verse or two but the structure of the New Testament itself; and the claim is NOT three gods — the persons share one undivided essence, one will, one power.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: It reaches that the persons of the one God are really and eternally distinct — one God undivided in being, never three gods. It does NOT reach a dissolution of the mystery: it answers the tritheism charge, not the further puzzle of how one being is three persons, and the analogies all limp (water’s states are modalism; three men are tritheism).

cards.q: Why is the baptism (Matthew 3:16–17) the scene modalism cannot stage?
cards.a: All three are present at once: the Son comes up from the water, the Spirit descends as a dove, the Father’s voice speaks about him — “this is my beloved Son.” A single actor changes masks between scenes but cannot wear all three at once and converse across them. Omnipresence explains how one person is in three places, not how he addresses himself as another.

cards.q: How does Gethsemane cut against modalism WITHOUT implying two divine wills?
cards.a: “Not my will, but yours” is the incarnate Son’s genuine HUMAN will freely yielding to the one divine will he eternally shares with the Father — not two divine wills, still less two gods. The anti-modalism point rests on the real address: the Son prays TO the Father, a person truly distinct from him, one who is really other — the whole point against modalism.

cards.q: Why does John 17:5 reach behind the incarnation?
cards.a: The petitioner asks for “the glory that I had with you before the world existed” and was loved “before the foundation of the world” (17:24) — before any human nature existed to do the addressing. So he cannot be the human nature speaking to indwelling deity; he is the pre-existent divine Son. And he says he HAD glory “with you” — a shared possession, not a place in a plan.

Jesus invokes the law requiring two witnesses and counts: “I bear witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me.” One person in two modes is, by Jesus’ own cited law, one witness testifying twice, and his argument collapses — it works only if Father and Son are genuinely two. (Natures do not testify; persons do.)

cards.q: Reply to: “I and the Father are one” — and “whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
cards.a: “One” in John 10:30 is neuter (hen) — one thing, one unity — not masculine “one person”; and 14:9–10 explains itself: “I am IN the Father and the Father is IN me,” mutual indwelling of two, not identity of one. The same discourse has the Son praying to, sent by, and returning to the Father — a reading must survive its own chapter.

cards.q: Reply to: Isaiah 9:6 calls the Son “Everlasting Father.”
cards.a: The Hebrew is “Father of eternity” — Semitic idiom for source or possessor, as Jabal is “the father of those who dwell in tents” (Genesis 4:20) and Eliakim “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isaiah 22:21). It is a role-title in a list of role-titles (“Wonderful Counselor,” “Prince of Peace”): it names what the Son is to his people, not which person he is. The persons are distinct; the perfections — eternity included — are shared.

cards.q: Reply to: the prayers were his human nature addressing his divine nature.
cards.a: Natures do not talk — persons do; “nature” is a what, and whats neither love nor listen. And the texts refuse the split: the Son asks for glory HE HAD with the Father before the world existed (17:5), loved before creation (17:24) — before any human nature existed to do the praying. Not foreknown, but HAD, “with you”: a shared possession, not a place in a plan.

cards.q: Reply to: three persons who love and send one another are three gods.
cards.a: What makes many gods is separable essences — Zeus and Poseidon have distinct natures, wills, and turf and can act against each other. The persons share one undivided essence, one will, one power; nothing is parcelled out, which is why the church rejected tritheism wherever it appeared. This answers the tritheism charge, not the further puzzle of how one being is three persons. To refute modalism by drifting into tritheism trades one error for its opposite.

cards.q: What does modalism cost — and does this case deny Oneness believers’ sincerity?
cards.a: It has no eternal Beloved to point to: the Son’s prayers become soliloquy, Calvary a monologue, and the salvation that brings us into the Son’s communion with the Father has nowhere to bring us. And no — Oneness believers are sincere and devout; the view should be engaged, not sneered at (1 Peter 3:15) — engaged as the serious error the case shows it to be.

obj.q: Jesus commands baptism “in the name” — singular — “of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Yet the apostles, who heard him, baptized “in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 2:38; cf. 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). The single name behind the three titles is Jesus — because Father, Son, and Spirit are one God whose saving name is Jesus.
obj.model: The Oneness case leans hardest on this text, so it needs a full answer. “In the name of Jesus Christ” in Acts is most naturally read not as a liturgical formula competing with Matthew 28:19 but as a description of Christian baptism — baptism into allegiance to Jesus as Lord, marking converts off from John’s baptism and from the synagogue. Luke records varied wording (“in the name of the Lord Jesus,” “in the name of Jesus Christ”), which tells against a fixed verbal formula. And the inference Oneness draws — that Father, Son, and Spirit are therefore one person — simply does not follow: that three share one name can equally express the unity of three persons in one God, which is how the church has always read Jesus’ striking singular “in the name” in Matthew 28:19.

obj.q: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and to Philip, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” These are not careful statements of two-in-one-essence — they are plain identifications. To see Jesus IS to see the Father, because Jesus simply IS the Father made visible.
obj.model: Read the grammar and the next clause: “one” in 10:30 is NEUTER (hen) — one thing, one unity — not masculine “one person”; and 14:9–10 explains itself: seeing the Son reveals the Father because “I am IN the Father and the Father is IN me” — mutual indwelling of two, not identity of one. The Son is the perfect image and revelation of the Father, not the Father himself. And the same discourse has the Son praying to, sent by, and returning to the Father — a reading of John 14:9 that erases the distinction cannot survive its own chapter.

obj.q: Gethsemane and the prayers are no problem for us: the genuine HUMAN nature of Jesus is addressing the deity indwelling him — flesh speaking to the Spirit within a single person. No second divine person is needed.
obj.model: Natures do not talk — PERSONS do; “nature” is a what, and whats neither love nor listen. And the texts refuse the split: the Son asks for the glory HE HAD with the Father before the world existed (17:5) — the divine pre-existent one is the petitioner; the Father loved HIM before creation (17:24) — before any human nature existed to do the praying. Oneness teachers reply that the glory of 17:5 existed only in God’s plan. But he does not say he was foreknown; he says he HAD glory “with you” (17:5) — a shared possession, not a place in a plan.

obj.q: Be honest — three persons who love, send, and submit to one another are three gods by any working definition. Oneness took the Shema seriously; you embroidered it. (Dale Tuggy presses this version not toward modalism but toward a strict unitarianism in which God is the Father alone.)
obj.model: Working definitions matter: gods are counted by separable essences — Zeus and Poseidon, rival wills, divisible turf. The persons have ONE undivided essence, one will, one power; nothing is parcelled — which is why the church rejected tritheism wherever it appeared, and why the Athanasian Creed insists on “neither confounding the persons, nor dividing the substance.” This answers the tritheism charge, not the further puzzle of how one being is three persons — which the doctrine does not claim to dissolve. Oneness “preserves” the Shema by deleting the New Testament’s data — the witnesses, the sending, the pre-creation love. And mark the cost once more: in saving the arithmetic you spend the gospel. The Trinity lets “God is love” and the Father’s love for the Son before the world stand together; modalism has no eternal Beloved to point to — and a salvation that brings us into the Son’s communion with the Father has, on your theory, nowhere to bring us.

unseen.q: “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). If ALL the fullness of deity is in Jesus, what is left over to be a separate person called the Father? Scripture itself puts the whole Godhead in Christ.
unseen.model: This text the orthodox affirm without reservation: Jesus is fully and completely God — “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” tells us that Christ lacks nothing of Godhood. What it does not tell us is that there is no distinct person of the Father. Full deity in the Son and a distinct person of the Father are not rivals: the Son is not a second instance of deity but the one God, eternally the Son, sharing with the Father one undivided essence — never torn off from it, never a lesser degree of it. The full deity of the Son is precisely what Nicaea defends. And the same Paul who wrote Colossians 2:9 opened the very letter by thanking “God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Colossians 1:3) — so the fullness that dwells in Christ does not erase the Father Paul addresses in the same breath.
